Thank you, Madam Speaker. I would like to make a few comments on Bill C-231.
We are called today to examine an issue which is not new by any means but which deserves a special attention. As a matter of fact, the issue of partisanship and political activities of federal civil servants is one that the Government has been thinking about for a fair period of time.
Public Employees Political Rights Act
At the turn of the century, a certain number of laws were passed in order to guarantee a neutral and impartial federal civil service. Thus, our civil service has gained an excellent reputation and respect because it was able to strike a proper balance between the rights of the individual civil servant and those of Canadian citizens who are entitled to a competent and impartial public administration.
At the present time, civil servants are not allowed to take an active part in certain aspects of our political process. As an example, they cannot publicly endorse any candidate. However, they can be candidates themselves with the authorization of the Public Service Comission. The PSC can refuse this authorization pursuant to section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act if it is of the opinion that his usefulness in his position would be impaired.
Public servants can also participate indirectly in the federal, provincial, or municipal process through contributions to political parties and their voting right.
The principle of non-active participation by public servants has been challenged in recent years, as you know. More so since special interest groups are demanding specific individual rights. During the 1984 federal election campaign this was made an issue by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). The issue was brought before the Federal Court seeking an injunction and to declare Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act unconstitutional. The injunction was denied. Together with a number of public servants the Hon. Member lodged a complaint before the trial division of the Federal Court of Canada. The case was heard in Ottawa in April of 1986, and in August of that year Mr. Justice Walsh delivered a 48-page decision. He clarified what public servants were allowed to do and what they were prohibited from doing within the scope of Section 32 of the Act. The Hon. Member was not happy with the decision, and this Bill comes as no surprise to any Member of the House, as he said a few minutes ago.

A person employed in a managerial or confidential capacity as defined by the regulation or a deputy head may exercise the right set out in Clause 4, subclause 1(a), and Clause 4, subclause 1(c).
Those two subclauses deal with the right to vote and the right to make financial or other contributions to a political Party. Considering that the regulation mentioned in Clause 4 is not determined, let us suppose that the criteria for determining managerial or confidential exclusions are the same as those in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Under that Act, approximately 7.5 per cent of all public servants are excluded for managerial or confidential reasons. If we take that figure

and add to it those public servants such as senior executives and managers, personnel administrators, and others employed in non-represented groups, we come up with a figure of approximately 10.5 per cent of the total Public Service for which the Treasury Board is the employer and who would not benefit from this Act. That means that one out of 10, or approximately 20,000 public servants, would be subjected to more restrictive legislation than we have now. Would we be able to claim this Bill would provide public servants with the fullest protection of freedom of expression as guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? I do not believe so.

That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of appointing a Royal Commission to investigate organized crime in Canada and to include in its report observations and recommendations on:
1.	the extent to which organized crime is present and active in Canada, particularly in such activities as drug trafficking and loan-sharking;
2.	the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of Canadian society;
3.	action taken by the government of other countries to investigate and curtail organized crime activity;
4.	legislation to enable the government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime;
5.	effective and appropriate punishment in instances of organized crime murder conspiracy; and
6.	possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses against organized crime.
She said: Madam Speaker, organized crime has been defined as:
Two or more persons consorting together on a continuing basis to participate in illegal activities, either directly or indirectly for gain.
This deliberate collaboration for illegal gain can develop into a self-perpetuating conspiracy that continues, despite what may happen to its original members, and that uses force and fear in its operations.
Organized crime has no ethnicity. It exists, it is pervasive, it is international in scope, and whether we know it or not, it is a fact of life. There is organized crime activity in loan-sharking, drug trafficking, robbery and extortion, activities that victimize innocent citizens. Organized crime does not exist as a separate subculture. It extends into our daily lives and the institutions of our society. The extent to which it does so is not known, and that is one of the reasons for my motion which proposes a Royal commission to investigate organized crime in Canada.
There has never been a national inquiry of this kind in Canada. There have, however, been provincial investigations. In Ontario in 1974, Judge Harry Waisberg's Royal Commission into certain sectors of the construction industry made some eye-opening revelations about the degree of corruption and organized crime involvement in Ontario's construction industry. Also in the 1970s, the reports of the Quebec crime probes extensively documented organized crime activity in that province.
The obvious conclusion, as I have said, is that organized crime is a fact of life, a force of corruption and a threat to our society. By its intrusion into other aspects of our lives, it is a threat to democracy. The issues it raises are national ones,

March 12, 1987
Organized Crime
which is why in my opinion a national investigation is called for.
Since organized crime exists to make money and buy power for those involved, it is clear that there is a good deal of money involved, many say billions, acquired illegally and outside the mainstream economy. Criminal organizations use modern financial services to conceal the illegal nature of their funds, to launder their money in other words. The increasing sophistication and the internationalization of the financial services industry make it extremely difficult to distinguish legal from illegal funds as transactions are processed in minutes through international financial networks.
In the United States in 1984, the interim report of the President's Commission on Organized Crime noted that the existence of modern financial institutions contributed to the frightening financial successes of organized crime in recent years. Without the means to launder money, organized crime could not flourish as it now does. I now have a very important ruling to make on a subject raised a few days ago by the Elon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).
On March 9, the Elon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) raised a question of privilege arising out of certain remarks made by the Honourable the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) in giving an interview to the press. The essence of the Hon. Member's complaint was that the Hon. Minister's remarks imputed motives to members of the Standing Committee on Employment and Immigration, that he questioned the right of the committee to put witnesses under oath, and that he appeared to be counselling a senior civil servant to defy the standing committee and the House.
I think I have caught completely the tenor and direction of the comments of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt.
A day or so later when it was possible for the President of the Treasury Board to be in the Chamber, he rose and agreed that he had been correctly reported in The Globe and Mail. I should perhaps repeat the exact words which form the subject of the complaint:
It is a terrible precedent. I would never ask a public servant to testify under oath. The committee is really saying he is a liar. I do not believe that... 1 would have liked to see Gaetan Lussier walk right out of the room.
There appears to be no argument that the Hon. Minister used those words.

The Hon. Member for Calgary West and the Hon. Member for Laprairie (Mr. Hawkes and Mr. Jourdenais), the Chairman and Vice-Chairman respectively of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, both contributed to the discussion and defended the committee's right to conduct its proceedings in the way it had. They also made it quite clear that in requiring certain witnesses to testify under oath, the committee was not implying that they were untrustworthy.
I must say, at the outset, that any parliamentary committee has the power to require witnesses to be sworn. I would also agree that in using this power, a committee is not reflecting adversely on the character of a witness. I can make the analogy with a Court of Law where all witnesses are examined
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
under oath. This necessary practice does not imply that all witnesses are dishonest.

I think it is important to emphasize, in case there should be any misconception in any quarter concerning the powers and functions of parliamentary committees, that committees appointed by this House are entitled to exercise all or any of the powers that this House delegates to them. These powers include the right not only to invite witnesses to appear but to summon them to appear, if necessary. They include the right to examine witnesses on oath should the committee deem it necessary. The powers of standing committees to initiate investigations have recently been extended in the spirit of parliamentary reform. Standing Order 96 sets out in some detail the extent of these powers, which include the power to study and report on all matters relating to the mandate, management and operation of departments of government. The scope of operations of standing committees has thus been considerably widened and the power to summon public servants as witnesses is essential to the effective performance of their tasks. It can be expected that this power will be used more, not less, frequently in the future, and I think it is salutary to alert all those concerned to this fact of parliamentary life. I can therefore say in answer to the question raised by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), that a witness once summoned by a parliamentary committee would be ill-advised to walk out because of an unwillingness to be sworn.

With regard to the existence of a question of privilege, I would remind the House that Parliamentary privilege is breached by any action which threatens freedom of speech in the House or which otherwise obstructs Hon. Members in the fulfillment of their duties. The Hon. Minister used certain words in his remarks to the press which expressed in forceful terms his opinion of a certain action by the committee. There is no doubt that these words were critical of the committee. However, it was not apparent to the Chair that the freedom of action of the committee or of any Hon. Member had been restricted by anything the Minister said. He was expressing an opinion, not giving an order to his public servants. In fact, the Hon. Member for Laprairie applauded the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) for defending his employees in such a spirited manner.

The Hon. Minister's words, which were no doubt delivered spontaneously, did nevertheless reflect upon the committee's actions. The limits of parliamentary privilege are very narrow and have never been precisely defined. Privilege should never be interpreted in such a way as to be an obstacle to the free expression of opinion. At the same time, we all need to be careful in our choice of language when speaking of the legitimate proceedings of the House or its committees.

Although the Chair finds no prima facie evidence of a question of privilege in this case, it is always wise to avoid offending those susceptibilities which can lead Hon. Members to raise complaints of this nature.
I want Hon. Members to take note of the fact that the Chair has very carefully examined the context in which the words of the Minister were spoken. Madam Speaker, in the few minutes remaining in private Members' hour, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on the motion sponsored by a very distinguished private Member of this House, the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). His motion has given us an opportunity today to look at the broad issue of Senate reform, a subject that has received considerable attention over the years, probably starting on July 2, 1867.
The Prime Minister of that day, our first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, coined the phrase "sober second thought". I think it is clear, although it is certainly a moot point, that from Confederation to the present day the Senate has made an important contribution in the area of legislative review. But the Fathers of Confederation also intended that the Senate should have a regional representation function. They used the expression "sectional interests" as being protected. I think few of us would deny that the second
principle function intended for the Senate is not being carried out effectively.
Why is it that the Senate is not able to play an effective role in regional representation? Again, there is broad agreement in this House, and I think across the country, that for Senators to be appointed by the federal Government until age 75 lessens the ability of Senators to represent their regions. As pointed out by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), the public does not accord a high level of legitimacy to Senators, largely because of the appointment method. As a result, the Senate lacks the authority to exercise the substantial powers it has under the Constitution. I think the Senators themselves, however willing and able they might be, are not seen as defending regional interests.
It seems quite clear that the principle purpose behind many recent proposals for Senate reform has been to restore to that chamber its intended role in regional representation. That is certainly one of the main aims of the Hon. Member from Prince Edward-Hastings. Some have pointed out that in the absence of a sufficiently strong second chamber, provincial Governments and Premiers have, on occasion, stepped in to try to fill that gap. Others have observed that our electoral system has created the impression that the support for national political Parties in particular regions is much lower than it really is. They also point out that in its present form the Senate cannot help to compensate for the imbalances in elected representation in this House.
There are other arguments for an enhanced regional representation role for the Senate, but in the end most of them share a common goal, to allow Canada's Senate to play the sort of role that second chambers play in other federal systems.
What is the evidence that improved regional representation has become the main focus of Senate reform proposals? I would suggest there is a substantial body of evidence to this effect, Madam Speaker. The former Special Joint Committee on Senate Reform was asked in its terms of reference, for example, to:
Report on ways by which the Senate of Canada could be reformed in order to strengthen its role in representing people from all regions of Canada.
The committee, as you know, heard many witnesses from various regions and sectors of Canadian society. Although their views and proposals differed, it is fair to say that more witnesses called for the Senate's regional representation role to be strengthened than for any other function to be emphasized.
In the remaining minute or so I would like to refer to one witness, a strong representative from western Canada, Dr. David Elton, President of the Canada West Foundation who said:
In this country what we really need are regional spokesmen in Ottawa, not provincial Governments per se, but regional spokesmen who can address the concerns of their constituents and ensure that they have a meaningful role to play in the deliberation and the legislation that the national Government brings into existence.
I appreciate that my time has expired and I thank the House for its attention, Madam Speaker.

BasePK: 3653987

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I thank the House for its indulgence. I will not be very long. I just wanted to put on record the full context of the background and the position of the federal Government for the benefit of Members and for the benefit of all Canadians.
If participants can achieve the level of agreement required for a constitutional amendment on aboriginal self-government, the federal Government believes that the door will have been opened to translating into reality the dreams of Canada's aboriginal peoples. In this sense, the Opposition's motion is not helpful as it is clearly not of a nature that could produce agreement to proceed with a constitutional amendment.

However, Madam Speaker, the Canadian Government's approach does not stop at that. Recently, we introduced a list of basic rules governing the financing of aboriginal governments.

Let me summarize what our approach does, Madam Speaker. First and foremost it asks that the aboriginal peoples of Canada give us none of their rights recognized within the Constitution. There are no risks in this regard for them. We
recognize those rights which are at present acknowledged by our Constitution.
Second, it provides for a solemn, indeed a constitutional commitment by governments to the aboriginal peoples that they will enter into negotiations aimed at concluding selfgovernment agreement.
Finally, it provides that the right to self-government identified in those agreements would be given constitutional protection. Let me stress what that means. It means protection in the highest law of this land.
Our approach would result in self-government arrangements based on negotiation and compromise. I think that is the route to follow in adjusting constitutional arrangements. I have to ask the question, and this, of course, is the nub of what we are talking about today: what does inherent right to self-government mean? Does it mean that we are going to dedicate the resolution of constitutional self-government to the courts and to a series of litigation by a variety of aboriginal peoples across Canada?
We have at the present time a very delicate and intricate jurisdictional relationship in Canada. It is appropriate and necessary for us to have a system which involves both levels of government in our country and the aboriginal peoples. Any amendment that would provide for an adjustment of those jurisdictional relationships must be formulated to ensure that that delicate balance is not thrown awry. The only way that I know of is through a process of doing it, what I call the Canadian way, through negotiation and agreement; a commitment to negotiate, a commitment with the aboriginal peoples enforceable in the courts of this land but nonetheless a political accord arrived at between the aboriginal people and the Governments of our country.
I agree with those who say that at the First Ministers' meeting we have a historic obligation no matter who we represent in those meetings to arrive at an agreement to set the basis for progress in the years ahead, to meet the legitimate hopes and aspirations of aboriginal peoples and to do it in a way which will ensure progress and ensure that the aboriginal peoples will realize self-government at the earliest possible moment in the most equitable way and in a way which will win the approval, not only of those peoples but of all peoples of Canada.
I thank you, Madam Speaker, for your time and for the indulgence of the House and I look forward to any questions that may be asked.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to sponsor today a Bill which is entitled "An Act to amend the National Defence Act". The purpose of the Bill is to amend the National Defence Act in order to remove all references to the death penalty for offences committed under the Act. A sentence of life imprisonment would replace all references to the death penalty.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, in 1976 this Parliament abolished the death penalty as far as the Criminal Code of Canada was concerned. The death penalty continues to exist in the National Defence Act and, as I indicated, the purpose of this Bill is to make the National Defence Act consistent with the Criminal Code of Canada. Capital punishment is wrong, whether it is in the Criminal Code of Canada or in the National Defence Act. Capital punishment is morally wrong whether it is done by hanging or by firing squad under the provisions of the National Defence Act.
Capital punishment is the mark of an indecent, uncivilized and immoral society. I regret very much that the Government is embarking upon a very divisive and emotionally charged debate on the issue of capital punishment with regard to the Criminal Code of Canada.
In closing I wish to indicate that the last time an individual was executed under the provisions of the National Defence Act was in 1945 during the Second World War. In the First World War 26 Canadian soldiers were executed by a firing squad for breaches of the provisions of the National Defence Act. This Bill will eliminate that possibility in future.

I have spoken to the people involved in the group, so I know of what I speak.
There should be a western economic development strategy. I know the Minister agrees with me in principle. Such a strategy should be based on three points. First, it should be based on
diversifying western Canada and building on the resource base and the agricultural base that already exist. I believe we can all agree that we have tremendous resources throughout the west, including great oil and gas resources in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Saskatchewan has immense potash reserves which represent about 30 per cent of the potash reserves in the world. There are tremendous forest resources throughout the Province of British Columbia and elsewhere in western Canada, and there are other resources in Manitoba and throughout the west. We need an economic strategy that will build on that particular foundation throughout western Canada and diversify the economy so there are jobs for western Canadians.
Second, we must build on agriculture in the west because of its great importance to our economy and the supply of food to the entire world.
Third, we need a change in transportation policy so that transportation will assist the western Canadian population rather than hinder it as it has done for so many years.
In addition to a western economic development strategy, I believe we must quickly take action to do more for agriculture if we want to save the family farm across the west. Let me put a couple of statistics on the record. We have heard about the real possibility of a drop in the initial price of wheat by some 20 per cent, after a drop in the price of wheat last year of about 19 per cent. If that happens, the price of wheat in this country for top quality grain will be some $2.83 a bushel. When one takes transportation to the Lakehead or the West Coast into account, top quality grains will produce some $2.37 a bushel. Let us compare that with the American farmer who receives $6.10 Canadian a bushel and the European farmer who receives $7 Canadian a bushel. How long can a farmer stay on the land at $2.37 a bushel in this country when the American farmer receives $6.10 and the European farmer receives $7? That is not good enough.
I have a study by the Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture which gives a breakdown of the cost of producing grain on a per acre basis. Again, the Department is talking about the impossibility of being able to even meet production costs in western Canada. The Saskatchewan Department of Agriculture says the farmer would have to produce an average of 58 bushels per acre of the top quality grain just to break even in the production of that grain, let alone meet the living costs of farmers and their families across western Canada today. When it comes to barley, it will be necessary to produce 135 bushels per acre if there is a drop of some 20 per cent in the price of barley, which everyone is predicting. Such production figures for the Prairies are absolutely unrealistic and impossible to meet. There are extremely serious problems in the grain economy, I suggest more serious than anything we saw in the 1930s. Farmers are receiving prices as low as $2.37 a bushel for the top quality grain and the price drops considerably for grades two, three, four and lower.
There are a number of ways to address the situation. First, we know that a major part of the problem is external because

Mr. Speaker, Revenue Canada is going as far back as 1983 to review the tax returns of hundreds of Canadian farmers who, in good faith, utilized the business investment tax credit on purchases of new farm machinery. When making a deal most farmers are interested only in the cash difference between the new item and the trade-in. They do not care how the paperwork is done. It is the cash difference that matters.
In cases where the dealer has exceeded the list or manufacturer's suggested retail price, there may be abuse and few would argue with that. However, the normal trade plus cash deal where the list price is not exceeded ought not to be the topic of a departmental witch-hunt. We certainly had hoped that the Minister, in tabling legislation dealing with the Judges Act, would bring forward the changes which were promised over a year ago. It is entirely in order, in speaking on a Bill to amend the Judges Act, to raise concerns with respect to other subject areas which might have been included at this point and which in fact have not. I know the Speaker recognizes that as well.
I would hope the Minister or his successor, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) would in fact live up to the promise made by his Government to bring forward a new appointments system at the earliest possible time. We recognize, particularly in dealing with some cases with complex socio-economic questions arising from the Charter of Rights, and in dealing with a review of Cabinet decisions-the courts can now review these decisions, after the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Cruise missile case-that it is essential that partisan political considerations not play a role in the appointments process.
I believe as well that in examining the nature of this process, the Bench should more accurately reflect the ethnic and multicultural diversity of our country. There should be more women appointed to the Bench. I would hope that the Supreme Court of Canada position which is now vacant would in fact be filled by one of the excellent women from the Province of Quebec who are eminently qualified to fill that position. I am pleased that the record of the Government with respect to the appointment of women has improved significantly. I am quite prepared to concede that and to concede as well how pleased I am, particularly in view of the fact that until this Government took office not one woman had been appointed by a Conservative Government to a federal judicial post in the history of the country. I welcome the progress which has been made in that regard.
To conclude, I want to reiterate our concern that the judicial appointments process in Canada must be changed. There must be a role for independent advisory bodies. There must, indeed, be a role for Parliament to play with respect to appointments to senior judicial positions at the Appellate Court level, the level of the Supreme Court of Canada. I would hope the Government would recognize its responsibilities in this regard and will move forward to quickly overhaul the judicial appointments process in Canada.
March 27, 1987

I share his concern, and I am eager to support any measure that would improve the safety of Canadian workplaces and the accountability of employers in the federal jurisdiction.
I will limit my comments to the safety and health implications of the motion, for I am very concerned about the appalling losses of life and property caused by industrial accidents. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, every year in this country about 1,000 workers die and many more are seriously injured because of workplace accidents and employment-related illnesses. In addition to the pain and suffering that

Unfortunately, I fear that the action suggested by this motion would not offer such a solution. In fact, it might reduce the efficiency of existing procedures under the Canada Labour Code for preventing potentially hazardous working conditions. It might even create an atmosphere of confrontation and hostility in certain workplaces, which would be both contrary to the goals and policies of this Government and itself a threat to workplace safety.
The Hon. Member's motion is intended to protect workers who resort to a practice known in labour affairs circles as "whistle blowing". The phrase implies that, if an employee knows that his or her employer is engaging in illegal, unscrupulous, or dangerous practices, he or she is not obliged to meekly go along with a course of action that is wrong, but may instead "blow the whistle"-that is, inform the authorities or the general public through the news media and thus help end the abuse.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the responsiblity of the law-abiding citizen to defend the public good does supersede the employee's loyalty to an unscrupulous employer.
But there are ways already provided in law for employees to report irregularities without inviting retaliatory action from the employer.
The majority of workers under federal jurisdiction belong to unions, and a union can bring strong pressure to bear on a delinquent employer. In most cases, a concerned worker would be best advised to inform his or her union of any irregularities such as are foreseen in this motion and rely on the established practices of the industrial relations system to correct the matter. The employee who complained would remain anonymous and so need not fear retaliation. Where safety and health are concerned, both unionized and non-unionized workers are protected by provisions of the Canada Labour Code that guarantee the right to refuse dangerous work.
Let me briefly describe what happens under present legislation when an employee believes that his or her employer is in violation of safety and health regulations or engaging in practices that could create, in the Hon. Member's words, "a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety". Section 85 of the Canada Labour Code states that, if an employee has reasonable cause to believe that a particular work process or condition could be dangerous to himself or any other employee, the employee has the right to refuse to do the work, without being subject to any disciplinary action or discriminatory treatment because of the refusal.
In certain cases, these conditions could have public safety implications. For example, a truck driver required to drive in excess of the maximum hours permissible under the Code may pose a threat to employee and public safety. There are
established steps that must be taken when an employee refuses to do dangerous work. First, the employee must inform the employer of the refusal to work and the reasons for it, and also report the incident to the workplace safety and health committee or representative. Second, the employer must then investigate the condition, along with the safety and health representative or a member of the committee. Third, if the condition is not corrected to the employee's satisfaction, a Canada Safety officer is to be called in to investigate the complaint. Fourth, if the employee is still not satisfied that the condition is safe or has been corrected, the matter may be referred to the Canada Labour Relations Board for adjudication.
Throughout this procedure, the employee is protected from dismissal or discriminatory treatment for refusing to work in dangerous conditions. The Canada Labour Relations Board has the authority to make the employer reinstate an employee who has been dismissed for this reason, rescind any disciplinary action, and repay any wages the employee may have lost because of the employer's discriminatory action.
Furthermore, under Section 72 of the Canada Labour Code, an employee who complains to the Minister of Labour about any irregular working conditions imposed by the employer may request that his or her identity be kept secret. Clearly, a worker who chooses, instead, to blow the whistle on his or her employer by reporting abuses to the news media cannot expect to remain anonymous. In short, Mr. Speaker, the intent of the Hon. Member's motion, insofar as it concerns circumstances under the purview of the Canada Labour Code, is already being adequately met by the existing legislation.
Furthermore, the measures recommended in the motion, if adopted by this House, could potentially disrupt the Government's whole approach to ensuring workplace safety and health. Mr. Speaker, Bill Reid, a world-renowned Haida artist, has reminded us that art is not simply a commodity which can be bought and sold or produced on demand. Art springs out of the life of an individual or of a people. As an artist, Bill Reid believes that when Canada refuses to recognize the legitimate rights of the Haida people, Canada has no right to display Haida art in its embassies around the world. BasePK: 3656205

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words I would like to say on this legislation. Because of the Government's majority there is no doubt this Bill will go through. However, the Government has not done what any good employer would do to make sure its employees are well treated. It is allowing this sale to take place in such a way that it will be branded as a Government that allowed employees of 25 or 35 years to be sold off with the company and without the same kind of pension plan they had before.
I have heard the protestations of government Members, but we are still faced with the fact that there are employees of Teleglobe who are not satisfied that they have been treated properly. They have put more into the pension plan than they are going to be able to take out. Those employees will receive $7 million less than they would have received had the Government made the same arrangement in this sale as it did in the sale of Canadian Arsenals.
Teleglobe was established in 1949. Since that time, with the infusion of public funds, it has grown. Yet with this legislation we are going to allow a private corporation to reap the benefit of that infusion of public money. That is quite unacceptable to most people. The taxpayer has the right to expect to get most of that money back. That has not been allowed to happen in this particular case, and a very profitable company will be sold to another operation which has very little experience in operating this type of company.
There is something else of concern to us. Here we have a monopoly operation and I am a little surprised that the free enterprise philosophy of the Government did not hold in this case. Ordinarily, if that philosophy did hold, the Government would have sold the company to Memotec and left it to the rough and tumble competition of the communications marketplace. Instead, this company will remain under the control of the CRTC, but with only a partial guarantee of a monopoly. That bothers the employees of Teleglobe as well. There will be quite an opportunity for other companies to bypass Teleglobe when it becomes a private organization.
The Government suggests that it will guarantee a monopoly to Teleglobe for at least five years. Even were that to hold true, and there is nothing in this Bill that says it will, what will happen after the five years? There are employees of this company who have given 15 and 20 years of their life who, five years from now, will be working for a company that does not have that protection and that may not have the expertise or power to survive in a free market-place.
There is also the matter of security. As my colleague from Winnipeg-Birds Hill said, every country in the world depends on a secure communications system in that they own and operate to a certain extent their communications with other
countries of the world. When Britain sold its overseas telecommunication operations it retained 51 per cent and control remains under British direction. Almost every country in the world is in a similar situation with the exception of the U.S. However, the U.S. has a parallel system operated by the military which is as effective or maybe even more effective than the private system on which it only partially depends.
We are not only giving away a corporation which could do quite a bit to reduce the deficit over the next few years, but we are putting ourselves in the position where we will be dependent upon a corporation which may or may not make a profit. In the end it may have to divest itself of some of its less profitable operations.
There are a number of issues in this sale which the Government has not dealt with in the legislation. It has not taken care to make sure that the employees are satisfied with the new organization, not only for today but into the future. The Government has not made sure that the corporation will continue to be successful. The Government has not even ensured that it will be able to operate profitably beyond the first five years.
The Government has decided that privatization under any circumstances is a good thing. It came to office almost three years ago with the conviction that the privatization of Crown corporations was good for Government and the country. From the day it came into power it began to do something about that conviction. The experience of privatization has not proven that that conviction was worth while following. The Government is now privatizing with no consideration for public interest or public policy but rather on an ideological conviction which it does not even bother to defend.
Canadians must be very concerned about the idea that the Government should not be involved in any enterprise that can be operated by the private sector. There are many areas of service in the country which it makes a lot of sense for the Government to operate. Admittedly, there are many operations in which it does not make sense for the Government to be involved, but there is an area in between, and in that area each divestiture should be examined closely. The divestiture of Teleglobe is one which should have been examined carefully. Through this transaction we are putting into the hands of a private corporation part of an industry which is important, not only to us in Canada but in our relationships with other countries.
If the Government continues its commitment to privatization, we will eventually put at risk the basic structure of Canada. In the West, for instance, we have private telephone companies in almost every province and private hydro companies in every province. All those companies operate well. Those kinds of services as well as international telecommunication services should be carried out by the public sector. Consequently, we in this Party will not be able to support this Bill when it finally comes to a vote.
March 30, 1987

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago when the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) announced that the Chileans blocked by him in Argentina were not refugees, that none of those people were refugees, my reaction was not to believe him. I did not believe him because I had personally spoken to a number of Chileans in Montreal who had arrived recently and who were seeking refugee status. They were people I would consider to be refugees. For instance, there was a lawyer who had worked for the Church in Chile and had been arrested several times. He finally decided to leave his country because he feared for his life.
There was a truck driver whose friends had taken part in demonstrations and who was therefore implicated through his association with these people. He too feared for his life and decided to leave his country. In the group in Montreal, at least among those I spoke to, there are people I consider to be refugees because I felt their stories had the ring of truth.
When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) said a few weeks ago that no one in Argentina was a refugee, I reached the conclusion that his assessment was not credible and that at least some of these people had a legitimate claim.
If the Minister had said that 20 or 25 were refugees, maybe half, I would have thought his assessment was credible. But when he says that no one is a refugee, I protest.
Since that time the facts have confirmed my feeling. Last week, the Quebec Minister of Immigration, after evaluating about 50 people, reached the conclusion that at least 10 of the people in question were in sufficiently precarious circumstances to be admitted to Quebec on humanitarian grounds. The Minister asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration to review those cases. I would like to point out that only those who asked to be allowed to settle in Quebec were evaluated by the Government of Quebec.
Then, Mr. Speaker, what has been the response of the Minister of Employment and Immigration? He says he is puzzled about the various assessments. You will admit Mr. Speaker that the Minister is disarming by naive. This confusing situation would justify a form decision on his part. He may have 56,000 assessments, Mr. Speaker, but the only one which really matters is his own, because he is the one who may admit these refugees in Canada. He is the only one who decides whether or not they have the right to enter this country.
Such a decision being so crucial and final-for this people it is a matter of life and death-it is imperative to ensure that those who are seeking refugee status may do so with a minimum of legal protection.
This is why recommendations made to the Government in recent years have been unanimous. People are asking for an independent, neutral and impartial procedure. Department of Immigration officials should not be expected to decide the fate of refugees because their responsibility is to administer the Immigration Act. These applications should be examined by people who are expert in refugee matters, and the Department of Immigration should not have anything to do with the whole process.
When applications are filed abroad .. . For example, the Chileans who have made headlines in recent weeks, who have been detained in Argentina, left stranded in Argentina by the Minister, these people in foreign countries are often in a predicament, separated from their families, facing an official who may not feel much sympathy for refugees, they have no access to legal advice, they have absolutely no right to appeal, they are at the mercy of the Minister of Immigration and his officials.
I therefore urge the Minister to admit that the refugee determination process in foreign lands has serious drawbacks. The Government should repeal the shameful measures imposed last February 20 and set up a compassionate and fair treatment system for refugees.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) reminded us that it was March 31, and he did so because he had a particular interest in that date. What I want to speak about today also reminds me that it is March 31, which means that tomorrow we are into the month of April, by the end of which we must have our income tax returns filed. Now is the time to be thinking about preparing our income tax returns.
Last week, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) about the federal sales tax credit that was introduced in the February 1986 Budget. This is a terrific program. Its purpose is to take into account the increase in federal sales tax while making sure that lower income Canadians are not penalized.
Because it is a new program, I have found that a lot of people who are eligible for it do not know about it. For that reason, I should like to take a few minutes to explain what the program is.
It is a tax credit program, and under it those with an income of less than $15,000 would be eligible for a tax credit of $50. For a family whose combined income is less than $15,000, a husband and wife who were living together as of the end of last year would be eligible for a tax credit of $100, plus $25 for each child.
This is a significant amount of money for lower income families, and we want to make sure that those who are eligible receive it. The point is, in order to get the credit, one has to file an income tax return. There are a number of people in this category whose incomes are such that they do not ordinarily pay any income tax and therefore do not file an income tax return.
I should like to refer to what was brought to my attention in my riding of Capilano. Senior citizens whose incomes were basically their old age pension, and perhaps the GIS, who do not ordinarily file income tax returns may not know that this year they should do so because they are probably eligible for the $50 credit. We want to make sure that people know about it.
Another category which has been brought to my attention is that of students. Every Canadian 18 years of age and over who is eligible and has an income of less than $15,000 should be filing an income tax form this year in order to obtain the particular credit.
I asked my question on March 25. I was pleased that the Minister of National Revenue in his usual way immediately issued a press release the next day-and I hope it has been well covered in the media-reminding people to claim their tax credit.

March 31, 1987
Adjournment Debate
As he said in the particular press release: "This tax credit is of particular importance to low-income Canadians, many of whom would not normally have to file a tax return". He emphasized that in order to claim the sales tax credit, a tax return must be filed.
That is the message we want to ensure that we get across. I hope all Hon. Members of the House will make the effort, through press releases and householders to their constituents, to ensure that the message gets out.
There is another point I want to raise because it was brought to my attention. There is some concern about people who have never filed tax returns. They are not used to it, they might be scared about it, and they do not know where to go for help. First I would advise them not to go to tax discounters. I was very pleased with the legislation we brought in last year to limit the role of tax discounters. It is not worth it, because there is help out there.
In my own riding of Capilano, British Columbia, I have worked with north shore seniors' groups and the information centre. In particular, the north shore health and information service provides volunteers to help seniors fill out their income tax returns. This is probably true across the country. There are many volunteers who will go to the homes of senior citizens and be in community centres to help with tax returns.
I was delighted by an article which was brought to my attention. It indicated that this kind of service was being offered by the Department of National Revenue. The particular project in Sydney, Nova Scotia seems to be an ideal one. I hope it is done right across the country. In the article Mr. Ross Crewe, Public Relations Manager for the Sydney District Office of Revenue Canada, talked about a program where Revenue Canada recruited all sorts of volunteers in the community to help people prepare their tax returns. If someone phones up, they will send a volunteer to the homes of seniors to help them. It does not have to be a scary kind of situation. It has some 70 volunteers in Sydney working out of a store-front office, so it is accessible. People do not have to climb a lot of stairs or go into a government office, which might be a little scary.
I should like to refer to some of the comments of people who have used the service. A gentleman, Mr. John Briand, said:
They say filling out the form is simple but it can be complicated . .. The

Speech:
Madam Speaker, in speaking to this motion, I would like first to congratulate the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for his continuous and courageous defence of the rights of the unborn child. I would also like to congratulate those who have spoken before me in favour of this motion. They have dealt with it in an eloquent and convincing manner on behalf of the unborn child. In particular, I would like to congratulate the seat-mate I first had when I came to the House, the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom), who on several occasions has spoken in support of the rights of the unborn child. I would also like to congratulate my present seat-mate, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson).
During my election campaign, a pro-life debate was held and candidates were asked to put forward their positions on the important question of the rights of unborn children. In that debate, I outlined three particular reasons for my position on this issue. I said first that I accepted that human life is different from other life forms on earth. Second, I said that on secular, philosophical grounds, I opposed the destruction of unborn children. I said that this is not a religious issue but that it is a human issue that crosses all societies and all races. In fact, one of the chief proponents of increased recognition of the rights of unborn Canadians, Dr. Bernard Nathanson, is a leading pro-life advocate in North America and opposes abortion because it is the arbitrary destruction of human life. Dr. Nathanson is an atheist.
The core of my opposition to abortion on demand is a conviction that this is a violation of the civil rights of the unborn child. In earlier speeches in the House and particularly in the speech I made on January 17, 1986, in support of a private Member's Bill I introduced, Bill C-254, I put forward the case for support for the biological reality of life before birth. I said that the unborn child can sense pain, can respond to sweetness and sourness and can move. I put forward a description of the existing legal rights of unborn children and I made it very clear to all Hon. Members that when I speak about the legal rights of unborn children, I am not introducing a novel concept. Our existing body of law, both criminal and civil, recognizes that the unborn child has legal rights that can be enforced and that are being enforced in the courts today. I outlined to Hon. Members the wide abuse of our criminal law prohibition against abortion. Notwithstanding the prohibition against abortion that exists in Canada, there is a practice which in fact is abortion on demand.
Today's debate which focuses on a motion that calls for the entrenchment of the rights of the unborn child in the Canadian Constitution is one that is being watched widely by my constituents. Before I entered the House to speak today, I discussed this issue with a rural constituent of mine, Francis De Lorey, a very strong and courageous advocate of the rights of the unborn child. I spoke with others as well.
Today I will not repeat the arguments I made on earlier occasions with respect to legal rights or medical evidence. In my view, none of that is seriously disputed. I want to take this opportunity to deal with what I believe to be a false premise on which those who advocate abortion on demand base their argument, and that premise is that we as human beings have the right to control our bodies. That argument has a certain superficial appeal, but let us think a bit about it.
What is that right to control our bodies? Does any Member of the House have the right to be kept out of jail for committing a crime? Of course not. We do not have that right because our right to control our bodies is limited by the greater social interests of enforcing certain criminal laws. That is why we can be brought before justice if we commit a crime. We can be arrested. Where is our right to control our bodies if we can be arrested? Where is our right to control our bodies if we can be physically searched? We have no absolute right to control our bodies. The right to control our bodies is a limited one. It is limited by the rights of others and by the greater social good. We see this in many situations. We cannot, for example, speak in an irresponsible way. We have free speech, but we cannot publicly condemn other people and make false statements. If we do we can be called before the civil courts and penalized.
The right to free speech is a limited right. Therefore, when I speak to the argument being put forward, which has so much superficial appeal, that a woman has the right to control her body, I think it is a false argument. It is not borne out by our legal system or by the decisions made on a daily basis concerning the rights of individuals. This Parliament and others have decided that our rights can sometimes be limited. In the case of the unborn, we are talking about the most basic of all rights, the right of that unborn child to live. It is interesting that we talk about an "unborn child". By definition a child is a person. We admit that a person exists before birth.
To conclude, it is time that we amended our Constitution to reflect the biological reality and the legal revolution taking place in our society which recognizes that biological reality. It is time that Canadian jurisprudence explicitly reflected the right of the unborn child to life. In doing so it will reflect the balancing of civil and legal rights which is an ongoing part of the evolution of our society. I urge all Hon. Members to support this motion when it comes to a vote.

The average Canadian has a great deal of difficulty understanding the very fine distinction the Minister has made. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in support of the motion proposed by my hon. colleague the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The purpose of the amendment is very clear. It is a very important amendment which I hope Members of this House will see fit to adopt. The Government is seeking to extend significantly the time during which patents will be protected, this despite the recommendation of the Eastman report. This legislation not only denies Canadian consumers new generic drugs for 10 years, but also denies them for seven years or eight years those drugs which are in the regulatory approval mill, in other words, generics which may have been licensed but not yet approved by the health protection branch. This amendment attempts to deal with that situation and was suggested by representatives of the Consumers' Association of Canada. It would amend Section 41.11 which says, in Subsection (4):
Subsection (1) does not apply in respect of any licence pertaining to a medicine where on June 27, 1986, a licence has been granted in respect of the medicine and a notice of compliance in respect of the medicine has been issued to the licensee.
This is in effect retroactive legislation. I recall Tories standing up in the House many times to express their strong and vigorous opposition to any notion of retroactivity in legislation. Yet by backdating this proposal to June 27, 1986, the Government is imposing that very thing. The amendment would make it clear that the restrictions in Section 41.11(1) do not apply if the compulsory licence or a notice of compliance had been granted by June 27, 1986, the date on which the first generic drug Bill was introduced. In other words, if the proposed generic drug was in the mill and being analysed by the health protection branch, these new provisions should not apply. Surely that is reasonable.

In suggesting the amendment the CAC said that where a company has received either a compulsory licence or a notice of compliance but not both, it is unfair to grant retroactive exclusivity of seven years to the patented drug. That is exactly what the Government is proposing. I suggest that the amendment is very sensible and will introduce some fairness and equity to this proposal.
Professor Eastman studied this issue exhaustively and with care. He examined some of the difficulties created when a patented drug has too long a period of protection. The Government's proposal is two and a half times the length that Professor Eastman recommended, and therefore it is important to remind the House and Canadians exactly what Professor Eastman said.
While it could be argued that this is a quite a complex and difficult issue, in many respects it is very straightforward. We are talking about the right of Canadians to low cost prescription drugs. We are talking about the right of Canadians to have a Government that will not cave in to pressure from multinational drug companies south of the border as part of a free trade deal. Every Member of this House remembers Clayton Yeutter's complaints about Canadian drug patent laws. We know the Government is caving in to that pressure. A period of 10 years for compulsory licensing is far too long.
My colleague from Winnipeg North has spoken on this point and led the fight, not just on behalf of this caucus but on behalf of all Canadians, against this Draconian legislation. I want to join with my colleague from Cowichan-Malahat- The Islands in saluting the work done by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). He is carrying on in the finest traditions of Members of Parliament from the north end of Winnipeg, including of course Stanley Knowles.

Patent protection may also be too long. This occurs when the period of patent protection is such that the innovator expects to earn profits in excess of the minimum necessary to justify the investment. Inventors' profits from innovation might on the average exceed the rate of return obtainable from other uses of the resources invested in research and development.
He then makes this comment:
Patent life also has an effect on the choice of research projects.
If the rewards of investment in research from the temporary monopoly are low, investment in marginal research projects, which are the least promising ones innovators carry on, are foregone even though their benefit for society would exceed the resources used.
He then makes this important point:
If average patent life is too long, it leads to a reduction in social welfare due to duplication and to overinvestment in marginal projects. The result of excessive patent protection is the attraction of too much investment in research and development and the consequent dissipation of the gains from research.
Innovating firms may be induced to compete for the high profits on new inventions by increasing their research activities with the result that the
discoveries of research which is marginally attractive to the firms bring negligible benefits for society.
In other words, new products do appear but the resources that have been spent to produce them would have benefited society more if they had been spent elsewhere. That argument by Professor Eastman is obviously a very powerful argument in terms of an undue delay in the area of patent protection. Certainly the suggestion of a 10-year period of patent protection is quite unreasonable.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I have ever asked you what it is that makes you wake up in the morning. I would like to know what it is. Perhaps it is the sunlight that streams through the window in the morning. Perhaps it is an alarm clock; or perhaps it is a clock-radio.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I am awakened by a clock-radio, and more often than not, it is not soft music that I awaken to but a loud authoritative news voice giving me some news and some comment, and usually the news, or at least part of it, includes a description of some very grisly crime that has occurred, and that authoritative news voice is telling me that we should be bringing back capital punishment. It berates those who oppose capital punishment or who are wavering a little on capital punishment in any way, shape or form.

April 7, 1987
Adjournment Debate
Last summer, Mr. Speaker, I, along with people right across Canada, woke up to news reports about a little girl in Toronto by the name of Allison Parrot. We first heard reports about her disappearance, and then we heard reports about her grisly murder.
This authoritative news voice kept telling us that we should be bringing back the death penalty. As a result of that urging, and all of those reports, there was in my constituency office, my office in Ottawa and my home, a deluge of requests to bring back the death penalty. I had an inundation of letters and telephone calls urging me to support the return of the death penalty, all the time pointing out that for many years the polls reflected support for the return of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, why is it that that happens so regularly? I do not know about you, Mr. Speaker, but I personally believe that that feeling was reflected in the comments of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Elnatyshyn) and the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario, and more recently in the comments of the Chairman of the Canadian Sentencing Commission, all of whom have said that Canadians have lost confidence in our criminal justice system.
The recent vigilante killings by store owners in Calgary and Montreal are yet further illustrations of that very point, that feeling of frustration on the part of the Canadian people. The Minister of Justice, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, also said that vigilante system is unacceptable; that a "Charles Bronson" system of justice is unacceptable.
I agree with those statements, Mr. Speaker, and I know you do, too. But, Mr. Speaker, it is the job of the Minister of Justice, the job of the provincial Attorneys General, to ensure that we have a system of justice in which Canadians can have confidence. Canadians must have confidence in their criminal justice system.
What is being done about it, Mr. Speaker? Of course, we are going to have a free vote on the issue of capital punishment. But, is that the answer? I doubt that you think so, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think so either. I believe that if the former Government, a Government that was in power for 15 years or more, had taken some action to tighten up the bail laws, as well as the sentencing and parole laws, we would not have this problem now, and Canadians would in fact have confidence in the criminal justice system.
Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I do that the present Government-bless it-cannot escape blame, either. Canadians voted for a change in September of 1984, and here we are today, insofar as the criminal justice system is concerned, and very little has been changed. In fact, we seem to be following the same old agenda. Perhaps it is the Liberal agenda, perhaps it is a bureaucratic agenda, but it is not the agenda of Canadians. Canadians know that between the years 1976 and 1985 violent crime increased 25.7 per cent in the country. They want the criminal justice system to be tightened up. I believe that public opinion polls would be very different now on the
question of capital punishment if steps had been taken to tighten up the criminal justice system.
Irrespective of whether capital punishment is brought back, Canadians want the system tightened up. The Minister of Justice would not have to worry about a vigilante or a Charles Bronson system of justice or about the confidence of Canadians in the criminal justice system if he would only tighten up the bail laws, sentencing, and parole.
The Minister and the Government have had some 2.5 years to do it. However, there are 2.5 years left in the mandate of the Government. That is enough time for the Minister of Justice to take some decisive action in this area so that he can leave a legacy of which he can be proud, of which I can be proud, and of which Canadians can be proud.
I am looking forward to hearing from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight that the Minister of Justice is about to take some decisive action and to leave a legacy of which all of us could be proud.

Mr. Speaker, work toward overcoming problems of farm finance and work toward overcoming problems of soil degradation must not be taken in isolation one from the other. I welcome the initiative taken by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and his Department to launch a major public awareness campaign related to soil conservation in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I too take great pleasure in speaking to the motion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Hees) would have liked to have been here because he has said on many occasions that not enough tribute has been paid to the role of the merchant navy in the Second World War.
The Merchant Marine was the lifeline stretching across the Atlantic. Weather, aircraft and U-boats threatened to snap that lifeline but, happily for all of us, it never broke. The Minister himself was a soldier who fought in the battle of the Scheldt. The purpose of that battle was to clear out the enemy so that the Port of Antwerp in Belgium would be opened to allied shipping. This was accomplished and the merchant fleets landed enough supplies to arm, fuel and feed the invasion forces. General Eisenhower said that Naziism was finished when the first ship sailed into Antwerp. Incidentally, it was a Canadian built vessel.
I thank the Hon. Member for allowing us to recall just how much the Armed Forces were dependent upon the merchant navy. The seamen manning those convoys were heroes, fully deserving of the House's time and attention today.
There is another group which also deserves our attention, the wives and girl-friends of those who went off to war. For many of them, the war meant loneliness and worry. A telegram could put an end to life's sweet young dreams. Many
had to bring up families alone, and a Fine job they did of raising a generation of young people.
I am glad this Government has been able to do something for these spouses. For instance, one of the first pieces of legislation introduced by the Minister included a measure to help recently bereaved widows or widowers of disability pensioners. Before the Minister acted, the money coming into the family was drastically reduced within 30 days of the death of the pensioner. One month there was a cheque reflecting the married rate; the next month it was the single rate.
We must think of the consequences, Mr. Speaker. The couple could well have had a large apartment on a long lease. Yes, Canada Works and the Canadian Jobs Strategy are good. They help the region. However, we are noticing that the number of dollars which the Government is allocating for the program is regularly declining and decreasing, so that fewer and fewer dollars are available while unemployment remains unacceptably high and well above the national average.
I should like to remind the House once again about a program for native people, an area of the economy where unemployment is particularly high. In 1984 the Native Economic Development Program was announced. It was to spend $345 million over four years in order to assist native people to cease being the recipients of social assistance and be able to have economic development programs which would make them self-sufficient.
Since that time only a fraction of the amount of money approved by Parliament has been consistently spent year by year. For example, in 1984-85, the first year of the present administration, Parliament approved $110 million for that program. Out of that $110 million, $102 million was allowed to lapse and only $8 million was spent. Obviously the Government is not even carrying out the will of the House in respect of where unemployment is highest, where people are suffering the most, where people are relying upon social assistance, hand-outs, and welfare, and where there is an opportunity for economic development. The Government allows a substantial

amount of money to lapse, and the people continue to be in the same state as they were before.

Mr. Speaker, I detected that there were actually two questions posed by the Hon. Member for
The Budget-Mr. Penner
Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). Before one o'clock I had talked about the decline in actual dollars in the regional development envelope. The decline is very serious. If you look at the Estimates you will find about a $3 billion decline which has been consistent since 1984-85.
As well, there is a cumulative effect. We have noticed in northern Ontario that for initiatives of various kinds, and we used to look to the regional development program for assistance, those dollars are no longer available. Some economists looking at our region have said that we really have to forget about having so much emphasis on big industry, on our forest sector, which is in some difficulty, to which I alluded, and on mining, which is in some difficulty because of depressed base metal prices throughout the world. The only exception is gold. I am grateful that we do have the Hemlo gold fields in the constituency of Cochrane-Superior, which is the one bright aspect, economically speaking. Economists have said that we are not looking at the existing possibilities for tourism in our magnificent region. We should be promoting tourism.
I am glad my whip asked me the question because I am going to extend an invitation to him in the next several weeks to join me on a fishing trip. If the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) behaves himself, I may even let him come along as well. I am inviting the Whip on a fishing trip and I will show him how great is the potential for tourism.
Here was a chance for the Minister of Finance in his Budget to have done something to encourage tourism in a region like northern Ontario. He could have said, "Yes, we want to encourage it". But what did he do? The Finance Minister added another 1 cent a litre to the price of gasoline; in addition to the previous 3 cents a litre we had in the last Budget. We have had a total of an extra 4 cents a litre or an extra 18 cents a gallon put on the price of gas when we already had the highest gasoline prices of any of the provinces of Canada. It is true that prices are higher in the far north. So, how is that an incentive for people who want to have a Canadian holiday somewhere in the great Canadian Shield? It is a disincentive.
If you want to fly on one of the charters at one of the main airports to a remote area for fishing-on a scheduled flight- you are stuck with another $4 on top of the ticket price. That is the contribution of the Minister of Finance to the encouragement of tourism in northern Ontario.
I repeat my theme once again. It is a simple one. We agree entirely with the Minister that some regions of this country are hurting, that the blow ought to be cushioned, but he gave us nothing at all to cushion the blow except a lot of sympathy, a lot of understanding, a lot of goodwill and many promises. But so far, Mr. Speaker, nothing in the way of action.

Mr. Speaker, I do not support capital punishment and, therefore, I oppose this resolution.

During the election the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a promise to the country that he would bring forward a free vote on capital punishment. We anticipated that that meant he would bring it forward in a clear, unequivocal
April 27, 1987

manner, that he would allow the House to divide, and that the consequences would flow from whatever vote we took.
Instead we have an attempt by the Prime Minister and the Government to disguise their real intentions. Instead of a straightforward motion on the death penalty they are trying to pass responsibility off to a committee of this House. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) told the House of Commons on February 13, when he brought in this motion, that the motion does not indicate that the Government supports or opposes the reinstatement of capital punishment. That position was echoed by the Parliamentary Secretary this morning. Yet the motion which he introduced, and on which we are asked to vote, begins with the words that you have recited, your Honour, "That this House supports, in principle, the reinstatement of capital punishment".
Who does the Government expect to fool-no position is being taken? Ministers are divided on the issue and are not taking responsibility for this motion-yet, the motion is quite clear that this House supports, in principle, the reinstatement of capital punishment.
The issue is to be turned over to a committee of the House of Commons. That committee will have the authority under the resolution to decide what crimes will be subject to capital punishment and what the style of that punishment will be. The committee will have the responsibility of preparing the actual Bill. All three of those items are vital; what crimes should be covered, in what way the ultimate punishment should be meted out, and the drafting of the Bill. That surely should have been the responsibility of the Government, or the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn).

Mr. Speaker, no government can resolve the issue of the death penalty by fence sitting, any more than we can execute someone partially. Either the death penalty exists in this country or it does not. The Government must put its cards on the table. The Government must clearly explain its position and take the consequences. But it doesn't want to do this. It wants to keep both sides happy.

To supporters of capital punishment they will say, "We have kept our word, we have brought it before the House". To those opposed to capital punishment they will say, "What could we do? The committee decided. It decided what crimes would be included, the style of the punishment, and it drafted the Bill."
This motion is sheer hypocrisy. It is a crass political move.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, there is not a subject matter more important for Members of Parliament to debate and deliberate upon than the one that is now
Capital Punishment
before us. As all members on both sides of this issue know, what is at stake here is whether this country will reintroduce into law the right of the state, calmly and deliberately, to take a human life.
It is the importance of this issue that leads me immediately to say to Members of all Parties that I intend to address my comments on this profoundly important matter, not to those who agree with me that capital punishment is wrong, but to those who are either undecided or, up to this moment, believe that it is appropriate for capital punishment to be reintroduced into our laws.
I have concerns about the origin of the resolution, the way it has been brought forward, and I have some concerns about the details of it. But I put those concerns aside to deal with the fundamental question that is at the root of the motion. As the right to experience life, Mr. Speaker, is the most basic of values, so too is the destruction of life, its denial to another, the most horrible of crimes. Whether that destruction is of a child or an elderly person, an invalid or an athlete, a scholar or a cab driver, a man or woman in the home, or whomever, whether that destruction is one of a random mass murder or an act that is premeditated and specific, the result, Mr. Speaker, is the same. The victim's life is snuffed out; it is finished, there is no more. The ultimate impingement on another human being has been carried out.
I am sure everyone in the House agrees that murder is horrible, that we must do all we can to prevent it, and that those who murder must in some sense be punished. However, these are not the central matters before us.
What is central is the obligation of those who want capital punishment to justify that course of action. What is central is their obligation, those who believe that killing our neighbour is morally wrong, to show that the same act of terminal violence when carried out by the state in the name of law is morally right.
Those who want us to approve of the motion, which in its essence, if established, would bring about the restoration of the death penalty, have the obligation to prove their case. If they want to take life, they must provide us with arguments which lead us to conclude that when sanctioned by the state the taking of a life is right.

People who are in favour of capital punishment have a moral duty to prove that killing by the State is justified and to argue their case. That is in fact the major moral concern of this debate, since a debate on the death penalty is about the right of the State to kill.
People who are in favour of capital punishment will have to provide moral arguments to justify the right of the State to kill a human being. In my opinion, killing is justifiable only in two situations. One is self-defence. If a man, woman or child is attacked by another person, he or she has a right to kill the

April 27, 1987
Capital Punishment
attacker, if necessary, to protect his or her life. The second is when a country or a state declares war or invades another country to forcibly impose its laws on it, thereby making use of violence and death. I think it is right and morally acceptable for the people of that country to defend themselves against the attacker.
The principle involved in these two examples is identical, Mr. Speaker. An individual has the right to protect his life when it is seriously threatened. A State or a community also has that right.

When the only defence against a violent attack on life is the use of violence, then that violence is morally justifiable. Individuals or states have the moral right to survive and to defend that survival when it is being assailed.
However, the question before us is of a different order entirely. It is whether the state is justified in killing a human being, not in active defence, but cruelly, deliberately, in a premeditated way, long after some crime has been committed. Those Members of Parliament who favour this premeditated destruction of human life by the state must make the case for it. It is their responsibility and theirs alone. They cannot shift the moral burden of justifying this kind of violence to those who elected them. They cannot claim they are merely following the wishes of the population.
